title: The Bridge of Nagasaki's harbor
premise: In 1938 Nagasaki, apprentice clockmaker Mirabel Sandoval is summoned to repair the harbor observatory's master clock, where she discovers a sealed letter hidden in its mechanism naming her own family in a smuggling plot that powerful men want buried. As war clouds gather and harbor authorities close in, Mirabel learns the plot's mastermind has arranged one secret berth on a departing ship — enough to save exactly one Sandoval from arrest. Torn between loyalty to her father, who orchestrated the scheme to pay her mother's debts, and the truth she owes the investigator slowly earning her trust, Mirabel must decide who escapes and whether survival purchased with silence is worth having. In the end she gives the berth to her younger brother, testifies to what she knows at devastating cost, and stays behind to rebuild — keeping time in a city that will soon need every memory it can hold.
about_author: A. M. Reyes is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloging port records across East Asia before turning to fiction. Reyes writes historical novels about ordinary people caught in machinery larger than themselves.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Gears
chapters.summary: Mirabel Sandoval arrives at Nagasaki's harbor observatory to repair its failing master clock, measuring her worth in tools carried and tolerances kept. Through her POV we learn of her family's debts and her father's strange new prosperity. The emotional beat is quiet pride shadowed by unease.

chapters.title: A Letter Sealed in Brass
chapters.summary: Deep inside the clock's housing, Mirabel finds a sealed letter naming the Sandoval family in a harbor smuggling operation. Terrified, she hides it rather than deliver it to the observatory director. Her POV; the beat shifts from curiosity to dread as the city's orderliness reveals its rot.

chapters.title: Father's New Coat
chapters.summary: Mirabel returns home and watches her father, Tomás, deflect questions about money while her brother Emilio begs for stories of ships. She says nothing about the letter. Family dinner scene from her POV; the beat is love strained by things unsaid.

chapters.title: The Investigator Who Winds Watches
chapters.summary: Harbor investigator Kenji Arai brings his own watch to Mirabel's shop for repair, probing gently about the observatory job. She lies badly. Alternating tension between attraction and suspicion; the beat is the first crack in her silence.

chapters.title: What the Harbor Remembers
chapters.summary: Mirabel follows her father at night to a warehouse on the docks and witnesses crates moving under false manifests. From her POV, the abstract crime becomes flesh. The beat is heartbreak: he is not a victim but an architect.

chapters.title: Confrontation at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Mirabel confronts Tomás, who confesses the smuggling was the only way to cover her mother's medical debts and insists the letter is a trap set by rivals. His POV dominates the scene. The beat is a father begging his daughter to choose family over truth.

chapters.title: The Man Who Owns the Tide Tables
chapters.summary: Mirabel is summoned by Colonel Vasquez, the plot's true mastermind, who reveals he knows she found the letter and offers protection in exchange for her silence and her skill fixing timing mechanisms for the shipments. Her POV; the beat is cold fear dressed as courtesy.

chapters.title: Gears Within Gears
chapters.summary: Mirabel repairs Vasquez's timing device while secretly memorizing its design, realizing it synchronizes the smuggling runs with patrol schedules. Her POV, meticulous and furious. The beat is agency born from captivity.

chapters.title: Kenji's Question
chapters.summary: Arai returns, no longer pretending his visits are about watches, and tells Mirabel three dockworkers have disappeared. He asks directly if she is afraid of someone. Her POV; the beat is the temptation of confession meeting the terror of consequence.

chapters.title: Emilio's Sea Fever
chapters.summary: Emilio announces he has taken work on a coastal freighter — one of Vasquez's ships. Mirabel realizes her brother is being pulled into the machine. Her POV watching him glow with excitement. The beat is dread sharpened into urgency.

chapters.title: The Berth
chapters.summary: Tomás reveals Vasquez has promised one berth on a ship leaving before the arrests begin — one Sandoval can vanish safely. The family argues over who it must be. Rotating POVs around the table. The beat is love turned cruel by arithmetic.

chapters.title: Mother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Mirabel finds her late mother's debt ledger and understands the full sum Tomás paid, and how many smaller families were ruined alongside theirs. Her POV, alone at night. The beat is grief that hardens into resolve.

chapters.title: A Watch Left Running
chapters.summary: Mirabel leaves Arai's repaired watch on his desk with a note containing only a date and a warehouse number — her first betrayal of her family for the truth. Her POV. The beat is terror and terrible relief in equal measure.

chapters.title: The Trap Closes
chapters.summary: Vasquez discovers the leak through a bribed clerk and gives Tomás an ultimatum: deliver his daughter or lose the berth entirely. Tomás's POV, torn between protecting Mirabel and obeying the man who owns them. The beat is a father's loyalty breaking against itself.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Mirabel and Tomás argue bitterly; he calls her testimony a second betrayal of their mother's memory, she calls his silence a slow murder of everyone Vasquez ruins. Both POVs interwoven. The beat is the theme made flesh: loyalty versus truth, with no clean side.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Ship
chapters.summary: Arai raids the warehouse based on Mirabel's information, but Vasquez anticipated it; the evidence burns and Arai is suspended. Mirabel learns her name is now on an arrest list. Her POV. The beat is despair — truth told too late buys nothing.

chapters.title: One Ticket, Three Names
chapters.summary: With hours left, the berth papers arrive bearing a blank name line. Tomás, Mirabel, and Emilio each try to write another's name. Rotating POVs. The climax's threshold: the beat is a family dismantling itself out of love.

chapters.title: The Last Berth
chapters.summary: Mirabel writes Emilio's name, forging her father's hand so he cannot refuse, and puts him on the ship before dawn. Tomás chooses to stay and face arrest beside her. Her POV. The emotional peak: sacrifice chosen, not assigned.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Mirabel testifies before naval investigators, surrendering her memorized timing designs and the original letter, which she had copied and hidden inside a customer's clock. Her POV, steady at last. The beat is truth as an act of craftsmanship — precise, costly, final.

chapters.title: The Fall of Colonel Vasquez
chapters.summary: Vasquez is arrested when the copied letter surfaces; Tomás receives a reduced sentence for cooperation. Arai, reinstated, stands with Mirabel outside the courthouse. Dual POV. The beat is justice arriving imperfectly, and gratitude that does not ask for more.

chapters.title: Letters Across Water
chapters.summary: Months later, Emilio writes from abroad; Mirabel reads his letters aloud to their father through prison glass. Her POV. The beat is tenderness sustained across distance — the price of survival counted in absence.

chapters.title: Keeping Time
chapters.summary: Mirabel takes over the observatory clock herself, winding it each dawn over a harbor that remembers everything. Final image: she carries little, but she carries all of it. Her POV. The resolution beat: memory as the only inheritance worth keeping.
